To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dinosaur tracks and lungfish aestivation borrows are reported from the Mesozoic of Bornholm.

we describe the oldest known dinosaur trackway in Denmark, which is a trample ground with 11 tracks, and that we report for the first time lungfish aestivation borrows from the lowermost Cretaceus of Denmark, which may be the oldest record of lungfish aestivation.
(i) the trampling ground was made by sauropod dinosaurs and (ii) the burrows are most likely made by lungfish.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: 1) the first report of dinosaur tracks and lungfish aestivation traces from the Danish Meszoic; 2) a new find of dinosaur tracks and burrows from the Berriasian Rabekke Formation of Bornholm; 3) a new interpretation of the depositional environment and palaeogeographical position of the Berriasian of Bornholm.
(1) dinosaur tracks and (2) lungfish aestivation traces, and (3) the environmental conditions during their formation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the trample ground and the burrows are the result of dinosaur and lungfish activity, respectively, in the shallow lake environment of the Skyttegard Member.
the dinosaur track and the possible lungfish burrow are the only two in-situ finds of vertebrate life from the Mesozoic of the Danish part of the Baltic Sea.

the dinosaur track and lungfish burrow-bearing mud was deposited in a shallow, coastal, freshwater lake, possibly in a low-lying area of a coastal plain, which was surrounded by a sparse, low-diversity, gymnospermous, riparian vegetation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Bornholm area during the Berriasian was a shallow coastal lake with an open, low-diversity vegetation, where sauropod dinosaurs occasionally came to drink and where lungfish occasionally dug aestivation burrows.
the Bornholm area during the Mesozoic was not a very attractive habitat for land vertebrates, and the few finds that have been made are probably due to local, temporary environmental conditions.
we have documented the presence of a small dinosaur population in a coastal environment, and we have found the first possible evidence of lungfish burrows in the Danish Mesozoics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Danish Mesozoics are not a barren period, but that vertebrate remains are rare and that the few finds of vertebrate tracks and burrows are of great interest.

it shows that it is still possible to find new and unexpected vertebrate fossils in Denmark, and it is hoped that the present report may stimulate more field work and research in Bornholm and elsewhere in Denmark.
it is not necessary to find vertebrate remains in order to infer their presence.
